hints: Focus on what balancing really means here, equal numbers of each atom on both sides with x = 4 and z = 2 already fixed.
Check the metals first, with 4 atoms on the left and 2 formula units on the right, see which equations give the same metal count.
Now balance oxygen last by finding y, remembering y must also be a whole number for the equation to count as balanced.
walkthrough:
**Set Up What x = 4 and z = 2 Means**

Great start, just plug the numbers in. You are testing if you can find a whole number y that makes atoms balance.

$$4\text{ metal} + y\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{ metal oxide}$$

**Test Equation 1 - Aluminium**

Left side has 4 Al atoms. Right side has $2 \times 2 = 4$ Al atoms, so aluminium balances perfectly.

For oxygen: $$2 \times 3 = 6 \text{ O atoms on right, so } y = 3$$
Since 3 is a whole number, equation 1 works: $4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.

**Test Equation 2 - Magnesium**

Left side has 4 Mg atoms. Right side has $2 \times 1 = 2$ Mg atoms.

They do not match, and x and z are fixed so you cannot change them. No value of y can fix the magnesium imbalance, so equation 2 fails.

**Test Equation 3 - Sodium**

Left side has 4 Na atoms. Right side has $2 \times 2 = 4$ Na atoms, so sodium balances perfectly.

For oxygen: $$2 \times 1 = 2 \text{ O atoms on right, so } y = 1$$
Since 1 is a whole number, equation 3 works: $4\text{Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_2\text{O}$.

**Conclude the Answer**

Equations 1 and 3 can both be balanced with a whole number y, while equation 2 cannot. That matches the option for 1 and 3.

options.A: Correct. Equation 1 gives $4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ with y = 3, and equation 3 gives $4\text{Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ with y = 1. Both have equal Al/Na and O on both sides with whole number y.
options.B: Incorrect because it leaves out equation 3. Students pick this if they correctly balance aluminium but forget to check sodium carefully. Equation 3 also balances with y = 1.
options.C: Incorrect. With x = 4 and z = 2, equation 2 is $4\text{Mg} + y\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}$. That is 4 Mg on the left but only 2 Mg on the right, so Mg can never balance no matter what y is.
options.D: Incorrect because it leaves out equation 1. Students pick this if they correctly balance sodium but think aluminium needs a fraction for y. In fact y = 3 works perfectly for $4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.
